_2: Peterson & Barney vowel targets the model already fits, so the two sets are comparable.
_why: The vowels have targets and a solver and score 10/10. The consonants had neither, which is
why a sweep came back 14/20 and why nothing had ever noticed that /n/ and /l/ share an F2 to
within ten hertz. Hand-placed postures are only as good as whoever placed them, and nothing
Sonorants first because they are the class this machinery already handles: they are voiced,
they have formants, and H.formants() measures them the same way it measures a vowel.
Fricatives want a spectral peak and a noise band instead, and stops want a burst spectrum —
different objectives, and they come after.
_tolerance: Every target carries a tol in hertz, and they are deliberately not uniform. F3 for /r/ is
the tightest in the set because F3 IS the English r/l distinction and a listener reported
exactly that confusion. Nasal F1 is loose because the murmur's first resonance is set by the
whole coupled system and varies more across speakers than the oral formants do.

sonorants.note: clear /l/, the prevocalic one. dark /l/ has a much lower F2 and is 8.7's problem.
F3 is the whole distinction from /l/ and carries the tightest tolerance here. Any American /r/ has it below about 1800; ours sits at 2410.

bounds.why: bunched or retroflex: the tip does the work, the body stays low, lips slightly rounded

sonorants.note: labio-VELAR: rounded lips AND a raised tongue body. Ours narrows only at the lips, which is why it was heard as /v/.

bounds.why: labio-velar: body high AND back, tip down, lips rounded. TWO constrictions, which is what it was missing

sonorants.note: the sound at the front of 'yes'. Reported correct by ear, and it measures correct — F2 2060 against 2070.

bounds.why: palatal: body high and front, tip down, lips unrounded

sonorants.note: the murmur. Place is carried mostly by F2 and by the antiresonance from the sealed oral branch.

bounds.why: sealed at the LIPS. the tongue is free, which is why /m/ carries so little place information of its own

sonorants.note: measured with the nose open it sits at F2 1250, still 450 low. Before the offline tract had a nasal cavity at all it read 1210, which happened to be /l/'s to within ten hertz — the right conclusion from the wrong measurement.

bounds.why: sealed at the alveolar RIDGE by the tongue tip, lips open

sonorants.note: F2 1090 with the nose open, against 1950 without one. The earlier reading put it 80 Hz from /j/ and explained a reported 'nya' that way; that was an artifact of measuring a sealed tube. The 'nya' is real and now unexplained.

bounds.why: sealed at the SOFT PALATE by the tongue body, at or in FRONT of the nasal junction at 0.44 — behind it the mouth shuts before the air can reach the nose, which is silence, and the solver found exactly that at 0.39. An earlier note here called 0.56 'too front for a velar'; that came from measuring a nasal with no nose and was wrong. The soft palate is just in front of the junction, because the junction IS the velum.

_bounds: Three formants underdetermine a tongue. Run without these and the solver hits every target
and gets there wrongly: it made /w/ with a FLAT body and a RAISED tip, which is the opposite
of a labio-velar, and made /j/ with the tip almost touching instead of a high front body.
That would not have been a cosmetic problem. Coarticulation moves whatever the posture
specifies, and since Phase 9 the PATH between postures is audible — a /w/ made with the tip
would drag the tip through every transition it takes part in.
So each sound carries the range its own articulators are allowed to be in. These are not
fitted; they are what the sound IS, and a solver that has to be told them is a solver being
asked a well-posed question instead of an ambiguous one.
_seal: A nasal seals the mouth completely and the PLACE of that seal is what tells /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/
apart. Formant targets do not say that — a shape can hit three numbers without closing at
all, and then it is not a nasal. So each carries a `seal` range: where along the tract the
narrowest point has to be, as a fraction. The solver rejects anything that does not shut, and
Same lesson as /w/, which the solver first built with a flat tongue and a raised tip because
three formants underdetermine a mouth. Targets say what a sound must SOUND like; they never
And the seal must be DOWNSTREAM of the velum. Shut the tract behind the junction and
the air never reaches the nose at all — the solver did that to /ŋ/ at 0.39, against a
junction at 0.44, and produced a sound with an rms of 0.0005. Silence, fitted perfectly.
_nasals: NASALS ARE FITTED ON THEIR ANTIFORMANT, not their formants. The murmur's formants come mostly
from the nasal cavity, which is the same cavity whatever the place of articulation — so /m/,
/n/ and /ŋ/ have broadly similar formants and are told apart by a ZERO instead.
The zero comes from the oral cavity in front of the seal, which is closed at the lips and open
at the junction: a side branch, and its quarter-wave resonance cancels. Seal at the lips and
that branch is the whole mouth, so the notch is low. Seal at the soft palate and there is
almost no branch left, so it is high or absent.
Fitting F2 for these was the wrong objective and it showed: the solver made /ŋ/ worse and
could not do better, because the number being asked for was not one the physics sets.
_fricatives: STAGE C. Fricatives are not fitted on formants — /f/, /v/, /θ/ and /ð/ all share an F2 of
1090, which is to say four of them are the same sound by that measure. Nor on postures alone:
/f/ and /v/ are byte-identical and should be, since they differ only in voicing.
What is wrong is the BALANCE between a voiced fricative's noise and its own voice. Measured in
/ʒ/ and /ð/ are almost entirely voice with a trace of frication on top, which is why one was
heard as /z/ and the other as 'a-loo-a'. Forcing them voiceless drops them to 0% and 1%: the
NOISE was always right, and the sustained measurements that said so were not wrong, they were
measuring a case where voicing is forced to a fixed level.
TWO KNOBS HAVE TO MOVE TOGETHER. Raising frication alone makes /ʒ/ louder than a vowel before
it makes it sound like a fricative — 116% of a vowel while still 58% voice. Cutting voicing
alone leaves too little noise to hear. The pair is the objective:
- low-band share near the voiceless partner's, plus what voicing should add
- level BELOW a vowel, since every fricative is quieter than one
which is two targets and two knobs, and wants solving rather than tuning by hand.
